text:
Pizza as we know it showed up in New York City around the early 1900s at Lombardi’s in Little Italy, though the city had precursors served in bakeries the previous century. Lombardi’s was followed by Patsy’s, Totonno’s, and John’s of Bleecker Street, all by baker disciples of Gennaro Lombardi. From there, the city’s pizzaioli continued to innovate, creating new varieties suited to the tastes and demands of customers.

Today, there’s a never-ending debate on where to find the city’s best pizzas. And while there’s no question that New York City is the nation’s capital of pizza, only a few have ascended to icon status. Here is a collection of pizzerias spanning all five boroughs, which every pizza-loving New Yorker should visit at least once.

For this update, we’ve added Andrea’s Pizzeria in the East Village, Jonny’s on the Lower East Side, and Il Leone in Park Slope. We’ve removed Pugsley’s, Arturo’s, and Lucia Pizza of Soho for now.

Open for: Lunch and dinner

Price range: $$$$ for whole pies

In an impossibly small Upper West Side space, the luscious square slices are on full display, each of them thicker, greasier, and more lushly topped than the one before. The crusts are crunchy, too, and the tomato sauce is slightly sweet. Note the stylish cupping pepperoni. The poached pear and gorgonzola square is unforgettable, and evidence of Mama’s originality. There’s another bigger location in the West Village.

Insider tip: The Uptown location feels more neighborhoody, while the West Village location hosts more pizza tourists.

Price range: $$

Giorgia Caporuscio — who won the title of pizza-maker of the year by 50 Top Pizza in 2024 — took over ownership of this Hell’s Kitchen restaurant from her father, the famous pizzaiolo Roberto Caporuscio. Look for a soft, doughy, and slightly charred pizza, best eaten with a knife and fork. One of the lures here is this deep-fried pizza called la montanara, with the toppings applied after frying.

Good to know: Giorgia is among the few women pizzaioli in the city.

Price range: $$$

John’s is one of the city’s oldest pizza operations, and it has retained much of its original New York character. Founded in 1929, the West Village restaurant churns out very thin, coal-oven-fired pizzas judiciously topped with sauce and cheese. Pizzas here are sold strictly by the pie (the awning says, “No slices”), with additional toppings like sliced meatballs, onions, ricotta, black olives, crushed garlic, pepperoni, ground sausage, and double mozzarella.

Good to know: Unlike many newer pizzerias, this one feels like a sit-down restaurant and offers beer and giant pours of wine. Even with that, the place is kid-friendly.

Price range: $$$-$$$$

Joe Pozzuoli opened this spot in 1975 in the Village, and today, it’s a champion of the New York slice. Joe’s has multiple locations around the city, as well as in Miami, Ann Arbor, and Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Good to know: Slices are between $4.50 and $6.50. It’s open until 3 a.m. weekdays or 4 a.m. weekends.

Open for: Dinner and weekend lunch

The team behind Bushwick favorite Ops brings its naturally leavened pizzas downtown with this East Village offshoot — and introduces a new style in the process. Inspired by co-owner Mike Fadem’s St. Louis childhood, the tavernetta pie uses a whole-wheat blend crust and spins out riffs like the Hawaiian or a classic for less than $20. For classic Ops orders, get the Rojo, topped with mortadella and pickled peppers, or a Mamma with meatballs and ricotta. This branch offers intriguing salads as well and a tight list of natural wines alongside cocktails.

Best for: The room isn’t quite as seductive as the original, but its location across from the Village East by Angelika movie theater makes it a great pre- or post-film stop — and one of the neighborhood’s most dependable new slice alternatives for a sit-down pie.

Open for: Lunch, dinner, and late-night

Price range: $-$$

Andrea Kenuti trained at Scarr’s and L’Industrie before opening this place. The shop offers New York-style and Sicilian pies, as well as garlic knots and calzones.

Good to know: The shop is name-checked by people really into pizza as one to watch.

Price range: $$$$

What began as a Bushwick apartment pop-up during the pandemic migrated to both locations of Superiority Burger, then landed full-time in Greenpoint about a year ago. Chris Hansell’s pizza project knows its way around a crust. His version tastes like the most classic of New York pizzas, a style that’s ubiquitous here, but he’s making pies with better ingredients and obsessive attention to detail. This newish pizzeria displays old-school vibes, movie-worthy interiors, and a great story in that it’s an homage to his late father, with whom he’d canvassed the five boroughs and beyond in search of the best pizza.

Keep in mind: There are no slices here.

Open for: Dinner

Open in one place or another — the Jersey shore, East Village, San Francisco, now the Lower East Side — since 1996, Una Pizza Napoletana produces some of the most perfect evocations of pizza in the Neapolitan style. These are smallish pies dappled with char, steaming straight from the oven. Only five or six different configurations are offered.

Take note: Neapolitan fans would agree this is the best pizza in the city. That makes it hard to get a table, particularly since it’s only open Thursday, Friday, and Saturday nights.

This new-wave slice shop with late-night hours sticks to classics: pepperoni, vodka, and plain slices. Characterized by its lightness, slices deliver a crisp crust via New York-style. Go for the vodka pesto or vodka pepperoni if you’re looking for a definitive slice.

Good to know: There’s also an intriguing turkey pesto sandwich with burrata on barbari bread.

Scarr’s Pizza swapped spaces, now found across from the original slice shop but still on the Lower East Side. Even though the new location is bigger than its humble beginnings at 750 square feet, customers sometimes still form lines. Owner Scarr Pimentel, who grinds his own flour, churns out what has often been described as a standard bearer for the perfect slice.

Good to know: A plain slice is $5, and specialty ones are around $7ish. It’s often a mob scene.
